## 6. RESPONSIBILITY REVISITED

In this section the focus will be on the equal opportunity principle in its responsibility-based version. A series of specific objections will be given, followed by an alternative proposal concerning the use of the concept of responsibility. This proposal will then be developed in the next section.

The first problem is that the philosophical basis of the equal opportunity principle is very fragile. By setting the cut between choice and involuntary circumstances, Arneson and Cohen bring to the fore a distinction which is highly problematic from a philosophical standpoint, and which many authors, including Dworkin, try to avoid. 12 Obviously, this approach'lands political philosophy in the morass of the free will problem' (Cohen 1989, p. 935). But Cohen continues:'We may indeed be 12 Although Dworkin's distinction between'brute luck' and'option luck' comes dangerously close to the same idea

## EQUAL OPPORTUNITY OR EQUAL SOCIAL OUTCOME

up to our necks in the free will problem, but that is just tough luck. It is not a reason for not following the argument where it goes' (p. 935). It seems to me that, at the very least, this point is nonetheless a serious handicap for the equal opportunity approach. As far as the application of the principle is concerned, we are left with two options. Either we wait for the free will issue to be settled by metaphysicians, although there is little hope that this will be done in the near future. 13 Or we allow political institutions to intervene to decide what factors the individuals are responsible for. 14 The trouble with this latter option is that the ethical value of the chosen allocations is then undermined, since it is almost certain that political decisions will not correctly address the metaphysical issue, and thus will not identify the true responsibility of individuals. Due to the complexity of the idea of responsibility, political institutions, lacking precise guidelines, are in danger of being influenced by social and cultural prejudices. History has revealed too many examples of the dangers of basing political decisions on fragile theological or metaphysical principles. Hence, it is unlikely that the result of a political selection of the factors for which individuals are held responsible would be even an approximate implementation of the equal opportunity principle.

Let us assume for a moment that this problem can be solved in one way or another, and that equal opportunity is tentatively enforced by adequate institutions. There may still be doubt about some individual's responsibility. In such a case, where does the burden of proof lie? Assume it lies on the responsibility side, that is, only when the individual's responsibility is proved must he bear the consequences of his decisions. If an incompatibilist view of free will were adopted, then any suspicion that there is causality would become a suspicion of nonresponsibility, and would lead to an egalitarian compensation. Now, in modern societies, determinism in human behavior occupies an important position in the Weltanschuung of most intellectuals and probably a large part of the population. 15 This implies that in any practical application the equal opportunity institutions would face a suspicion of nonresponsibility. As a result, it is likely that any application of equal opportunity based on an incompatibilist (not just a hard determinist) view of free will would amount to equalizing outcomes. On the other hand, a compabilist view of free will may raise another difficulty. The ethical appeal of the thesis that individuals must live with the consequences of their responsible acts, may not be completely independent of the concept of free will that is employed. In particular, the 13 The philosophical debate on free will is not even so much on whether there is free will or not as on what free will means (see, e.g., Van Inwagen 1983; Kane 1985). That it might be a self-contradictory notion is also a plausible thesis (Double 1991). 14 This idea is defended by Roemer (1993). 15 This is what Scanlon (1988) calls the Causal Thesis. See Scheffler 1991.

compatibilist project is mainly to justify attitudes of praise or dispraise (if not blame). To justify differences in welfare or in social success is quite another matter. Even if a compatibilist account may provide grounds for moral attitudes of praise and dispraise, it is more questionable whether it could justify differences of welfare or advantage between people. The presence of an identified deterministic factor explaining a person's behavior gives her very good arguments for complaining about any penalty in welfare or advantage imposed by equal opportunity institutions, or symmetrically, seriously undermines any claim to preferential treatment yielding a higher outcome. In brief, the equal opportunity approach faces a sort of dilemma: its ethical appeal is stronger with an incompatibilist view of free will than with a compatibilist one, but the doubt problem is then also more acute.

Now, even if we believe in a view of free will and moral responsibility justifying differential outcomes, our moral intuition can run into conflict with the principle of equal opportunity, as Bert's case should show. Bert has received a normal and balanced upbringing, but he has freely adopted a negligent and reckless character. In particular, he enjoys having his hair blown by the wind when he rides his motorbike on the highway, and he seldom wears a helmet even though he has one and it is compulsory to wear it. One morning he takes out his motorbike to pay a visit to his parents, and, on leaving them, spurns his mother's warnings about the helmet, saying:'I prefer to take the risk and enjoy the wind!' But on this particular morning, Bert's careless driving causes an accident, in which he suffers serious head injuries. The hospital diagnoses a trauma which requires a costly operation Bert cannot afford because he has no health insurance. He will die if nothing is done.

In this case, the equal opportunity principle would not endorse any transfer of resources to help Bert. He is fully responsible for his injury. 'When persons enjoy equal opportunity for welfare ... any actual inequality of welfare in the positions they reach is due to factors that lie within each individual's control. Thus, any such inequality will be nonproblematic from the standpoint of distributive equality' (Arneson 1989, p. 86). I hope Bert's example will make it clear how the word'any' can be frightening in this last sentence. If you freely and deliberately make the slightest mistake that can put you in a very hazardous situation, a society complying with equal opportunity will quietly let you die. If Bert had lost a finger, most people would probably think that he deserved it; but fewer people would agree with the'no transfer' verdict in the above case. It is not only whether Bert is responsible or not which matters, but also the amount of welfare loss he is about to suffer following his mistake. Admittedly, his punishment is indeed proportional to the degree of risk he has chosen, and he had envisioned the possible consequences of what he did and could have taken precautions against

## EQUAL OPPORTUNITY OR EQUAL SOCIAL OUTCOME

them. However, I believe that our ethical intuition may lead us to consider that the scale of penalties must not be so harsh. It seems that however criminal and stupid his behavior may have been, there is a limit to the kind and amount of suffering he should endure. Our society cures its criminals when they are injured, because this kind of physical penalty is not considered appropriate. In the light of this example, the equal opportunity principle looks rather primitive.

Cohen is as severe as Arneson, and the following passage shows it, but also suggests a defense of equal opportunity:'When deciding whether or not justice (as opposed to charity) requires redistribution, the egalitarian asks if someone with a disadvantage could have avoided it or could now overcome it. If he could have avoided it, he has no claim to compensation, from an egalitarian point of view'. (Cohen 1989, p. 920; see also p. 940) The defense of equal opportunity one could imagine from this passage is that what motivates a transfer to Bert is not an egalitarian justice standpoint, but either charity (as opposed to justice) or nonegalitarian justice considerations. I think such a defense would be very weak. To put the boundary between justice and charity at this point is merely a restatement of the equal opportunity principle, not an argument for it. Cohen's distinction between justice and charity is moreover highly questionable in itself. This kind of opposition was similarly exploited by Nozick (1974), for example, to vindicate a rejection of egalitarian transfers while agreeing with spontaneous charitable gifts. But charity considerations can become a topic of distributive justice if a community makes them a matter of public policy. It is obviously a matter of egalitarian distributive justice that the satisfaction of basic needs should be given priority in the distribution of resources. It is this idea that supports the thought that Bert should be helped. Let us assume that after his accident, Bert understands the foolish nature of his previous behavior. Let the individual who emerges from this understanding be called Bert II, as opposed to the negligent Bert I. If life could be lived again, Bert II would amend some of Bert I's decisions, including the driving behavior and the helmet wearing. The question is: should Bert II bear all the consequences of Bert I's follies? Again, the equal opportunity principle is dreadfully categorical on this issue.'People share equal opportunity for welfare just in case there is some time at which their opportunities are equal and if any inequalities in their opportunities at later times are due to their voluntary choice or differentially negligent behavior for which they are rightly deemed personally responsible' (Arneson 1989, p. 86). In simpler terms, the decisions you make now may condemn you for the rest of your life. Again, although this approach is perfectly coherent, I argue that it may shock our moral intuition. The change of personality and the fact that the new individual would not make the same decisions call for a revision of 16 the penalty. Possibly suspecting this problem, Arneson (1990, p. 179) looks for a mysterious'canonical moment' which separates childhood (age of nonresponsibility) from adulthood (age of responsibility). But there is no such canonical moment, and we must face this important anthropological fact that a human being is in a constant process of evolution and education. Even if one thinks that Bert II is still responsible for what Bert I did, it is not obvious that Bert II should be punished and suffer for something he would not now do. Does this objection simply demand a slight modification of the equal opportunity principle to allow for'sincere conversions'? The problem is deeper. The constant evolution of a person, be it smooth or sometimes sudden, dilutes the moral responsibility for her actions over time, so much so that the principle of equal opportunity should take that into account in its basic formulation. I would propose that at every moment m, you should face the welfare prospects (after transfer) that you would face if you had in the past made the decisions that at m you would be inclined to make if you were to live again all your life up to m. Obviouly, however, this idea seriously complicates the already impossible implementation of equal opportunity!

The equal opportunity principle cannot simply guarantee equal opportunities of expected welfare in the beginning of life, and must allow for correcting transfers after accidents and unpredicted random factors that affect the individual's prospects. Otherwise, it could not be true that 'any inequalities in their opportunities at later times are due to their voluntary choice or differentially negligent behavior' (Arneson, 1990, p. 179). Now consider a person whose expected welfare drops suddenly because of an unforeseen adverse random circumstance. He or she is clearly not responsible for this fact and, if the above argument is correct, will receive a compensatory transfer. But assume that if this random accident had not occurred, this person would have voluntarily taken a course of action leading to the same bad outcome. It is then less obvious that he or she still deserves to be compensated. One can consistently claim that such hypothetical actions are irrelevant, and that equal opportunity only analyzes actual events and their causes. But our ethical intuition may ask more. Imagine that a person is about to voluntarily drop his money into the river, but, one second before he does so, a sudden gust of wind snatches it out of his hands and deposits it in the water. A strict application of equal opportunity would compensate him, but is this a satisfactory solution? In order to avoid this kind of result, the 16 'When some convict is now less closely connected to himself than at the time of his crime, he deserves less punishment. If the connections are very weak, he may deserve none' (Parfit 1984, p. 326). It is a matter of fact that the punishment of criminals is commonly affected by their behavior after their indictment (during the trial as well as in jail), and by what this behavior reveals of the evolution of their personality. Again the equal opportunity principle looks more primitive than the current penal system.

## EQUAL OPPORTUNITY OR EQUAL SOCIAL OUTCOME

equal opportunity principle ought probably to contain a clause like this:

after an accident affecting the welfare prospects of the population, compensatory transfers ought only to bring the individuals back to the levels that they would have had but for the accident. The complexity of the equal opportunity principle seems unbounded.

There are further practical problems. In face of the free will problem, Cohen offers a'reassuring point'. We are not looking for an absolute distinction between presence and absence of genuine choice. The amount of genuineness that there is in a choice is a matter of degree, and egalitarian redress is indicated to the extent that a disadvantage does not reflect genuine choice. That extent is a function of several things, and there is no aspect of a person's situation which is wholly due to genuine choice' (Cohen, 1989, p. 934). This hardly sounds reassuring for the equal opportunity principle. 17 Imagine the debates in the Ethics Committee which would have to set the kind and cost of medical care that a person in Bert's situation would be allowed to receive free of charge, depending on her degree of responsibility ... If a matter of degree is introduced, issues of quantities will be raised, and this is an additional problem rather than a reassuring point. Confronted with the question of the informational difficulties implied by the equal opportunity principle, Arneson (1989, p. 87) suggests that, although obviously the outcome function is not known, and neither its shape nor the list of its arguments will ever be accessible, we have evidence of its gross features. This evidence enables us to apply equal opportunity in an approximate way. Equal opportunity is the ideal toward which we should direct our efforts. But this approximation method makes sense only if there is some continuity in the process, that ensures that any refinement of our knowledge of the outcome function and its arguments can lead the actual allocation of resources closer to equal opportunity. However, nothing is less plausible. The structure of the equal opportunity principle is such that, whenever there is some imperfection in the information about the outcome function or the observed variables, the allocation chosen to implement a gross equal opportunity can be quite far from the ideal allocation. If one discovers some event in Bert's childhood which explains his negligent attitude, the size of the transfer made to him will be increased dramatically. If afterwards one finds out that a gene in his DNA should have helped him correct this problem, the transfer will be taken away. And so on.

Being very fragile in its theoretical basis, completely untractable and substantially undesirable, the equal opportunity principle suffers from the drawbacks of the concept of responsibility it relies upon. Is this just 17 'Hi! I'm from the Ministry of Equality. If, by any chance, you are unusually unhappy today, you will receive an allowance of x% of what would compensate you if you can prove that you are less than (100 -x)% responsible.' See Cohen, 1989, p. 910.

'tough luck'? Is there no other acceptable solution between a restrictive resource-egalitarianism (equal r's) and a comprehensive outcome-egalitarianism (equal O's)? It seems to me that most of the arguments and intuitions put forward by factor-selective egalitarians, and in particular the proponents of equal opportunity, can be salvaged and used in a more tractable way if one acknowledges the twofold meaning of the concept of responsibility.

In ordinary language, the word'responsibility' is used in (at least) two different contexts. You can be'responsible' for your act, and this is the meaning exploited by the equal opportunity approach. But it is also said that some issues, such as the furniture in your house or the way your children are raised, or national policy if you are chief of government, are your'responsibility'. In social life, decision-making responsibility over all the facts and things that have to be decided is distributed to various agents: individuals, groups, organizations. Every individual takes part in a variety of such decision processes, and this delineates his or her area of responsibility. Contrary to how it may appear at first glance, decisionmaking responsibility does not have anything to do with free will. This is a purely descriptive concept that is used to describe how a society allocates the power of decision to its members, and no particular explanation needs to be given of how and why specific decisions are made. A hard determinist view of the world would not remove the fact that the way I dress is my own daily responsibility. Probably my choice is influenced by many factors, including the remarks of my fellows, but whatever happens at the moment I pick my clothes from the closet, I remain, from the viewpoint of society, the decision maker in this domain. This is simply what this concept of responsibility means. It involves an idea of authority as well as an idea of obligation or duty. 18 Now, this second concept of responsibility may capture some of the intuitions that motivate selective egalitarianism, and on this basis a different criterion can be proposed. This is the topic of the next two sections.

7.

## OUTCOME-SELECTIVE EGALITARIANISM

Given the flaws of factor-selective egalitarianism, I propose directing our attention to morally relevant aspects of outcomes. The idea is the following. Factor-selective egalitarianism considers a comprehensive individual outcome O, identifies all the factors that affect this outcome O = O(a,f3,...), and sorts these factors into three categories: r, t and w. This approach may be appropriate for a lot of practical competitive problems, from sport to trade regulations, but, as shown above, it is not 18 The idea of duty also leads to a third use of the word, as in the phrase'responsible behavior'.

## EQUAL OPPORTUNITY OR EQUAL SOCIAL OUTCOME

satisfactory as far as global issues of distributive justice are concerned. In this latter field, my proposal would be to draw a list of all relevant outcomes which depict an individual's fate (health, living standard, education level, career, family life, sense development, preference satisfaction, cheerfulness, etc.). O becomes a vector (O a, Op,...), whose components are the various outcomes, which may also be identified with Sen's notion of'functionings' (Sen 1985). Then, for each of these outcomes or functionings, it must be decided what decision centers (government, local authorities, associations, family and friends ... and last but not least, the individual herself) should assume some responsibility for the achievement obtained by the individual.'Responsibility' is here understood in its second meaning, and no idea of moral desert is involved. Now, the particular responsibility of social institutions would be to achieve equality across individuals, in the outcomes for which these institutions are responsible.

In short, I propose shifting from factor-selective to outcome-selective egalitarianism. And to make a very crude but convenient simplification, let us assume that only two decision centers are distinguished, society and the individual. Then the components of O would fall into two categories O = (O\,O2)-The first one would include all of the outcomes for which society assumes some responsibility, and the second-type outcomes would be left to the entire responsibility of the individual and his circle of close relatives. A society based on this outcome-selective egalitarianism would design a set of institutions aiming at equality in the outcomes of the first category, and the outcomes of the second category would be disregarded in this respect. The designers of such egalitarian institutions would probably be given some way of aggregating the various outcomes which are under the (partial) responsibility of society: if a unique index ip existed, these institutions would seek to equalize y(0i) across the individuals. But it is very likely that such an aggregation would be difficult or even undesirable. This is not a serious handicap as long as the inequalities are substantial enough to make the direction of required change obvious. When it is not obvious, this probably means that the inequalities are so minor that the equalization itself loses its importance.

In other words, in this simplified but convenient framework, a boundary would be drawn between individual outcomes submitted to egalitarian care, and individual outcomes of purely private interest. Let us call'social outcomes' the individual outcomes of the first type, that is, the components of O\, and'private outcomes' the components of O2. The precise location of such a boundary may partly be a matter of public debate. An intermediate degree of responsibility might also be assumed by society with respect to some private outcomes. For these outcomes society would not guarantee equality, but would only check that their individual levels belong to some defined interval. The level they have within the interval would be a private matter, but they would give rise to social concern as soon as they move outside the bounds of the interval. That may happen for instance in the enforcement of Mill's proviso discussed below. At first glance, this general proposal might seem compatible with the equal opportunity principle and the notion of responsibility it conveys. The private outcomes could be those that individuals genuinely control, whereas social outcomes could be those for which the individuals cannot be held responsible (first sense). In other words, responsibility in the first sense might be a precondition for granting responsibility in the second sense to an individual. This idea, however, cannot be accepted for at least three reasons. First, a factor-based selection and an outcome-based selection are totally different. An outcome-selective egalitarian principle does not use any information concerning the causes of the individuals' behavior or results. 19 Indeed, I propose equalizing social outcomes independently of the degree of control the individuals have, and disregarding private outcomes even if inherited handicaps affect individuals in this respect. The second reason is the following. Were such information available, it would not make sense to examine whether an individual is responsible (first sense) or not for an outcome. Responsibility in the first sense only concerns factors, that is, contributions to outcomes, but not the outcomes themselves. If O — O(x, y) and I control only x, I cannot be held responsible for the outcome O, but only for the factor x. If y is fixed and I change x, then I may be held responsible only for the variation of O. But I cannot take responsibility (first sense) for O in general, whereas I can be given full responsibility over O in the second sense. Bert is not morally responsible for his health in general, but only for his peculiar behavior. Therefore it is impossible to select private outcomes on the basis of individual responsibility (first sense). The third reason is that what motivates the proposal of giving a sphere of personal responsibility (second sense) to individuals within the outcome-selective framework has nothing to do with genuine control and free will. This point is developed below.

A very obvious practical drawback of equal opportunity is that it requires that all facilities and subsidies devoted to helping particular handicaps or expensive activities should distinguish between the beneficiaries depending on whether they have genuinely chosen this handicap or activity, or have inherited it by chance. Mecca pilgrims would have to declare the origin of their faith, and those who have converted to Islam knowing the cost of travel to Mecca would pay full fare. The community

19 More precisely, it needs only to know the impact of r over O so as to compute the adequate allocation, but it need not make any distinction of the t/w type.

## EQUAL OPPORTUNITY OR EQUAL SOCIAL OUTCOME

photography facility would refuse access to those who have genuinely chosen to practice photography. Such a system is not only practicably impossible, but looks ethically questionable. Should the fact that a person has'genuinely' chosen to become a Muslim or a photographer imply that he ought to be excluded from the social help given to other Muslims and photographers? The principle of equalizing social outcomes is much more reasonable in this respect, since it would oppose any filtering in such circumstances.

The advocates of equal opportunity are very concerned with the possible exploitation of egalitarian institutions by individuals squandering social resources. This possibility is real, and an egalitarian society cannot look upon such practices without doing something. But the response should not be to punish the culprits by simply refusing them any further help. It would be more appropriate to implement safeguards (for example, vouchers may be a safer means of aid than cash), education and incentives, in order to make wasteful behavior less easy or less desirable.

For most social outcomes, the individual makes the essential contribution and social institutions simply play the role of a safety net. Equality of social outcomes may remove a part of individual incentive, but four channels of incentives remain. First, equality should in fact be interpreted as maximin, and contrary to pure egalitarianism, maximin precludes redistribution schemes which induce destructive behavior lowering everybody's outcome. Second, it is likely that the safety net will be quite global and not just for each detailed outcome. For instance, if I want a high income I must earn it, because social help will not bring my income up to the level I desire. Third, there exist incentives for cooperation that do not fit the homo economicus model, although, empirically, they prove to be quite strong, and an egalitarian social environment may help individuals to develop cooperative behavior. Fourth, private outcomes (like pride, happiness) may be influenced by the contribution of the individual to his or her own social outcomes. The possible inequality in those outcomes leaves room for direct individualistic incentives.

Does the outcome-selective approach escape from the problems of factor-selective egalitarianism and equal opportunity described in Sections 3 through 5? No separability condition emerges from the idea of equalizing social outcomes. If, for instance, there is some influence of O\ (or its factors) over O2, this does not raise a problem because O2 is not supervised by the social institutions. Concerning the incompatibility between ERET and efficiency, the idea of individual responsibility over personal tastes, in the second sense of'responsibility', is naturally compatible with the idea of freedom to trade goods in order to adapt the allocation to personal tastes: the precise bundle consumed by a person may be under her responsibility as well as her own tastes. At least, it would not make any sense to stipulate that, because the personal tastes belong to O2, the allocation of resources should not be adapted to them. Finally, externalities and interactions between individuals' actions and outcomes do not raise any particular problem for an outcome-selective approach. The fundamental question of why some outcomes should be private and should not be taken care of by social institutions remains to be addressed. In this respect, Scanlon's Tanner Lectures 20 suggest an appealing answer. Scanlon detects in the use of the word'choice' an ambiguity similar to that in the word'responsibility". Choice may denote either a past act or a range of opportunities. It may be important to give people a substantial amount of choice (= responsibility, second sense), without their particular act of choice implying any moral desert (= responsibility, first sense). The fact that some outcomes should be private, then, stems from the fact that it is essential to preserve a substantial degree of choice and autonomy in individuals' lives.'Just institutions must make outcomes depend on individuals' choices because of the importance which individuals reasonably attach to this dependence. ... The value of choice is not a purely instrumental value. People reasonably attach intrinsic significance to having outcomes depend on their choices' (p. 189). The intrinsic'value of choice' can then be a basis for a distinction between social and private outcomes. If a comprehensive outcome such as welfare or advantage were systematically equalized by society, the individuals would lose their autonomy in spheres such as preference formation and satisfaction, subjective happiness, etc. 21 20 21 Scanlon, 1988. Scanlon actually proposes this'value of choice' approach as an alternative to w h a t he calls the'forfeiture view', which is very close to the equal opportunity principle. However, t w o points m a y be worth mentioning. First, his criticism of the'forfeiture view' is rather weak, and unfortunately relies on the assumption that only conscious choice morally matters in that view, whereas Arneson's equal opportunity principle allows for negligent behavior to be penalized a s well. Second, he applies the'value of choice' approach to cases of hazard warning in a n unpalatable way. H e argues that people w h o d o not take account of warnings and suffer damages should not b e rescued, because by warning t h e m w e h a v e p u t them in sufficiently good conditions of choice. Such a view is in fact compatible with equal opportunity and the'forfeiture view', but not, I believe, with the'value of choice' approach or equal social outcome. Because the choice which is offered in this example is not, as Scanlon says, the'good' choice of avoiding d a m a g e b y following the warning advice, but the'bad' choice of either avoiding d a m a g e or suffering damage, which is not the kind of choice that h a s t o b e promoted. A s Scanlon admits,'one w o u l d prefer to eliminate these outcomes altogether if that were possible' (1988, p. 190). Moreover, the individuals suffering damage have a reduced range of opportunities in their life, afterwards, due to diminished health and life expectancy. If choice and opportunities must be promoted and equalized, these individuals need some help. Their past act is irrelevant for the'value of choice' approach.

## EQUAL OPPORTUNITY OR EQUAL SOCIAL OUTCOME

The'value of choice' approach is helpful in clarifying some important details of the equal social outcome principle. First, it supports the above remark that it may be desirable that individuals' initiative make a substantial contribution to the social outcomes they achieve. The social institutions must deprive individuals of as little autonomy as possible, and only take care of inequalities in final outcomes. Second, even if a global composite outcome is equalized, it may be crucial that individual choice should prevail in determining in detail how the components of the global outcome are filled for everybody (the global outcome is'social' while it consists of a set of private outcomes). Third, in all domains, including private choices, it is the responsibility of social institutions to fight against undesirable influences and to provide the individuals with good conditions for choice. The purpose is not to make sure that choices are genuine and that agents are morally responsible for them (first sense), but instead to enhance choice as a factor of quality of life for all individuals.

A second reason for the selection of private outcomes is that a private sphere must be preserved from any public scrutiny and social intervention. In particular, the basic liberties of thought, speech and movement imply that the outcomes directly concerned with thought, speech and movement should not elicit any intervention. One can probably go further, although maybe not as far as J. S. Mill, who qualified as private all the acts concerning only the self (Mill 1910; Riley 1989). On the other hand, Mill's proviso concerning a possible harm to others should probably be retained. If some private outcomes may be harmful to other persons, then some measures of social prevention should be adopted. For instance, the way I dress is my responsibility, but some eccentric options might be harmful in some ways to other persons in society, and it may then be reasonable to put some limits on the extent of my authority in this respect. A defense of privacy on slightly different grounds is put forth by Rawls (1982). A complete equalization of an overall outcome such as welfare or advantage would rely on an ordering of individual outcomes which would not fully respect the independent and incommensurable values of the different goals and life plans of the individuals. This idea is related to the well-known'bare persons' objection, but we need not go as far as discussing the monist eudemonistic feature of equal welfare, for instance, as Rawls does. In order to defend the principle of a private sphere, all that is necessary is that a comprehensive assessment of a person's success in life should not be made from the central viewpoint of social institutions. Only a partial and basic assessment should be performed at this level, and the rest belongs to individual goals and particularities. This is a third reason for purring some outcomes into the private sphere.

A fourth reason is also proposed by Rawls. The means available to individuals, and their achievements, should not be held up by the unreasonable demands of others. In particular,'strong feelings and zealous aspirations for certain goals do not, as such, give people a claim upon social resources, or a claim to design public institutions so as to achieve these goals. Desires and wants, however intense, are not by themselves reasons in matters of justice' (1982, p. 171). A natural way to protect the individuals from such unreasonable demands is to give all of them responsibility over their own goals and degree of satisfaction. The distinction between private and social outcome might help understand an apparent contradiction that Cohen finds in Rawls's theory. On the one hand, Rawls defends the idea of primary goods on the grounds that people are partially the masters of their preferences: "The use of primary goods ... relies on a capacity to assume responsibility for our ends' (Rawls, 1982, p. 169) On the other hand, Rawls objects to rewarding effort and desert because'the effort a person is willing to make is influenced by his natural abilities and skills and the alternatives open to him. The better endowed are more likely, other things being equal, to strive conscientiously, and there seems to be no way to discount for their greater good fortune' (Rawls, 1971, p. 312). Cohen notices that this suggests a double standard in the treatment of responsibility. A partial responsibility in tastes, according to Rawls, entails no compensation (as if people had a one hundred per cent responsibility), whereas a partial responsibility in effort would lead to a total compensation (as if people had a zero per cent responsibility). Maybe in Rawls's mind, the idea was mainly to make the allocation of primary goods independent of both effort and tastes because in both cases we are unable to determine the degree of genuine personal choice. But in view of the above arguments, another interpretation is possible. There is no reason to subsidize particular tastes insofar as this remains a private matter, that is, they typically belong to the domain of individual responsibility. In contrast, some of the rewards that a person might receive due to her effort are likely to fall into the cluster of social outcomes. And the principle of making social outcomes depend on genuine personal choice (as opposed to circumstances) is much more problematic than the principle of making private outcomes depend on personal choice. A society which does not directly intervene to counter the deterministic factors influencing private outcomes is simply a society which respects privacy. Whereas a society which sets out to distinguish circumstances and choice in order to allot social rewards will run into all the troubles described in the previous section.

In addition to the'value of choice' and the privacy arguments, there might be other reasons for putting some personal outcomes into the private cluster. For instance, height is usually considered a private

## EQUAL OPPORTUNITY OR EQUAL SOCIAL OUTCOME

outcome in our society. An individual who happens to be rather small, or rather tall, can obtain no compensation for this (within certain limits of size). However, this is an outcome that individuals can hardly modify, so that choice (genuine choice or Scanlon-type choice) cannot justify this fact.

And individuals are seldom indifferent about their size; it affects their welfare and advantage (some jobs even require a particular size).

Nonetheless, I doubt that this situation should be deemed socially unfair, and it is not clear that we would like equality in this outcome (a uniform size for all individuals in the population) or compensation for this by other means. The same could probably be said about beauty, intelligence, etc. In conclusion, there may exist outcomes that are relatively important for the welfare of individuals even though their unequal distribution is not in itself a matter of social justice. 22 A possible reason for this fact might be a concern to respect the person. A direct social valuation of the individual's physical features or characteristics would undermine her self-esteem, and a principle for a just society might be that such differences between individuals do not matter in themselves. From the standpoint of justice, they matter only insofar as they impair the performances of individuals in their participation in social life.

We must then take issue with the claim that if hard determinism is adopted, full equality of welfare or advantage must ensue. None of the five above arguments is affected by hard determinism. The existence of a private sphere is desirable independently of the free will issue. Outcomeselective egalitarian institutions provide no compensation for any brute bad luck affecting an individual's private outcome, but this is not as harsh as it may seem. Either we simply do not care about inequalities in such outcomes, or we consider it more important not to interfere with individual autonomy in this field.

In view of the reasons for the existence of a private sphere, a few suggestions can be made about outcomes that can reasonably be put into the private cluster. First, due to the first four arguments, the life-style and consumption of individuals should be a private matter, although, of course, Mill's proviso should also apply to circumscribe the effects of externalities. Second, apart from considerations of mental health and education level, I would suggest putting all subjective and intellectual outcomes into the private sphere. This implies respect for basic liberties, but it also concerns the formation and revision of preferences and goals, and their degree of satisfaction. Third, as developed above, respect for the person should preclude any public scrutiny over natural physical characteristics of persons. Notice that even if most subjective outcomes remain private, that

22 By contrast, related consequences of such handicaps may call for social help as soon as social outcomes are affected. Loneliness and illiteracy demand some intervention, but not ugliness and stupidity which may cause them.

does not mean that subjective problems will not elicit social help. They will do so, however, only if they have consequences for social outcomes. For instance, if cheerfulness is deemed a private matter, the person who is naturally sad, but otherwise leads a perfectly normal life, will not be compensated with any social resources. Similarly, the naturally cheerful person would not be penalized for this trait of personality. But if their social outcomes (job, income, family life, for instance) are affected, then social institutions may intervene. In contrast, since none of them has chosen to be sad or joyful, equal opportunity would immediately subsidize the former and tax the latter.

The case of expensive tastes can be dealt with in a similar way. It is not because Louis has chosen to cultivate a taste for plover's eggs and ancient claret 23 that he will not receive a subsidy, but rather because he has been given by the institutions, a personal autonomy over his tastes and the satisfaction of these tastes. The reasons why he develops such tastes are not to be scrutinized, unless they interfere with social outcomes (for instance, not to be threatened or manipulated would probably be a social outcome). It may also be decided that some particular tastes (for example, for alcohol, tobacco) would belong to Q\ and would trigger some intervention and help (probably not a consumption subsidy), independently of the degree of choice involved in such tastes. The problem of adaptive tastes can be addressed in a similar way.

Another suggestion can be made, now concerning social outcomes. A very important individual outcome indeed seems to be respect for the private sphere, as has been argued above, and it would fall under the responsibility of social institutions to guarantee such respect. Notice that the exact content of this particular'social outcome' would depend on the definition of the private sphere, which can vary to some extent in different societies.

Equal social outcome is then a principle which potentially gets rid of most of the informational problems implied by equal opportunity. The reason is that outcomes are much more easily observed than causal factors. Moreover, all of the relevant social outcomes could probably be chosen to be easily observable, especially if the most subjective outcomes (satisfaction, happiness) are put into the private sphere. No serious ethical limitation seems to be entailed by such an observability condition. Some problems of interpersonal comparison might however arise: how can we compare the career achievements of a plumber and of a lawyer? But I would claim that such problems are less tricky and more sociologically relevant than the factor analysis and welfare comparisons required by factor-selective egalitarianism.

23 See Dworkin 1981a, p. 229; this famous example is due to Arrow.

## EQUAL OPPORTUNITY OR EQUAL SOCIAL OUTCOME

8.

The equal social outcome view is, in brief, a combination of Rawls's and Sen's theories. With Sen and against Rawls, it focuses on functionings and not on goods, because ability differentials are an important source of unjust inequalities amongst individuals. But with Rawls and against Sen, it argues that social institutions should not take care of the fate of individuals in a comprehensive way. 24 Only the distribution of social outcomes, which might also be named'primary functionings' in this perspective, matters from the standpoint of social justice. Another essential difference with Sen is that functionings are the relevant variables, instead of capabilities, which imply an idea of moral responsibility. As an illustration, an application of the equal social outcome approach which would seem plausible to me for western societies, would select only six individual outcomes: respect for the private sphere (denoted s, for each individual /, hereafter), health (hi), education and information (e,), wealth (we,), collective decision-making power (p,), social integration (avoiding loneliness, si,-). Applying the maximin criterion to an index of these six individual outcomes, that is, would be a tractable framework for egalitarian policies. This is just an example, and of course many details have to be worked out concerning the measurement of these six variables, and the shape of the index tp.

I will conclude with two general remarks. First, the definition of the variable s,, respect for the private sphere, can follow two very different approaches. The first one, adopted for instance by J. S. Mill, considers individual autonomy as isolation and independence of the individual from social influences and interventions. This approach is relevant as far as specific institutions (such as the state) are concerned, and the usual definition of basic liberties can rely on this view without any problem. But in a broader sense of individual autonomy, this approach is quite naive, as pointed out by Schoeman (1992), because individual life cannot be lived in isolation from a social context, and for an individual, increasing one's degree of isolation is more often impoverishing than liberating. An alternative view of individual autonomy can be built on the fact that belonging to various independent groups, in various spheres of life, is a basic guarantee against excessive dependency on a particular social group. Enhancing respect for the private sphere may then consist in encouraging multiple social integration rather than in hindering collective 24 In Sen's theory, subjective satisfaction is for instance an important functioning to be taken into account.

institutions. In addition to these considerations, Scanlon's'quality of choice' and individual self-expression can also be observed and fostered in many ways by various social institutions.

The last point is that, as can be seen in the above example with six social outcomes, it may be impossible to implement a precise distribution of some social outcomes (such as education, wealth, power) without seriously reducing individual freedom of choice (of life-style, for instance). One might think that this problem requires the introduction of choice sets or capabilities, instead of functionings. But then we are back into the morass of free choice and of the metaphysics of moral responsibility. I do not, however, believe that this is necessary. Indeed, if there is a trade-off between the distribution of some social outcomes and the respect of the private sphere, such a trade-off can be directly reflected in the index tp or any similar tool, and the implementation of a distribution of individual values of <p is simply a matter of economic analysis, similar to what is done in the theory of optimal taxation. To admit such a trade-off seems more sensible than to consider that differences of individual levels in some basic functionings do not matter provided they reflect choices. I would rather say that such differences always matter, but that they may be tolerated when respect for the private sphere is at stake.

## FERREIRA GIGNOUX 2011 THE MEASUREMENT OF INEQUALITY OF OPPORTUNITY

**Source file:** `md_extractions/FERREIRA_GIGNOUX_2011_THE MEASUREMENT OF INEQUALITY OF OPPORTUNITY.md`

# Review of Income and Wealth

Series 57, Number 4, December 2011

DOI: 10.1111/j.1475-4991.2011.00467.x

roiw_467 622..657 THE MEASUREMENT OF INEQUALITY OF OPPORTUNITY: THEORY AND AN APPLICATION TO LATIN AMERICA by Francisco H. G. Ferreira*

The World Bank and IZA and

Jérémie Gignoux

Paris School of Economics Building on the existing literature, this paper constructs a simple scalar measure of inequality of opportunity and applies it to six Latin American countries. The measure—which captures betweengroup inequality when groups are defined exclusively on the basis of predetermined circumstances—is shown to yield a lower-bound estimate of true inequality of opportunity. Absolute and relative versions of the index are defined, and alternative parametric and non-parametric methods are employed to generate robust estimates. In the application to Latin America, we find inequality of opportunity shares ranging from one quarter to one half of total consumption inequality. An opportunity-deprivation profile that identifies the worst-off types in each society is also formally defined, and described for the same six countries. In three of them, 100 percent of the opportunity-deprived were found to be indigenous or Afro-descendants.

JEL Codes: D31, D63, J62

Keywords: inequality of opportunity, Latin America

1. Introduction Economic inequality—usually measured in terms of income or consumption—is neither all bad nor all good. Most people view income gaps that arise from the application of different levels of effort as less objectionable than those that are due, say, to racial discrimination. Indeed, the distinction between inequalities due to the exercise of individual responsibility on the one hand, and those due to predetermined circumstances on the other, has become central to the Note: We are grateful to Caridad Araujo, Pranab Bardhan, Ricardo Paes de Barros, Marc Fleurbaey, James Foster, Markus Goldstein, Stephen Jenkins, Peter Lanjouw, Marta Menéndez, Vito Peragine, John Roemer, Jaime Saavedra, and three anonymous referees for helpful comments on earlier drafts. Insightful comments were also received at conferences or seminars at the World Bank, the IDB, the Brookings Institution, Cornell University, the Catholic University of Milan, Universidad de los Andes in Bogotá, Colégio de México, Universidad Torcuato di Tella in Buenos Aires, and the Universities of Essex, London, Lund, Manchester, and Oxford. We also thank Carlos Becerra, Jofre Calderón, and Leo Gasparini for kindly providing us with access to data. The views expressed in the paper are those of the authors, and should not be attributed to the World Bank, their Executive Directors, or the countries they represent. *Correspondence to: Francisco H. G. Ferreira, The World Bank, 1818 H Street NW, Washington, DC 20433, USA (fferreira@worldbank.org).

Review of Income and Wealth © 2011 International Association for Research in Income and Wealth Malden, MA, 02148, USA.

Review of Income and Wealth, Series 57, Number 4, December 2011 literature on social justice in political philosophy, social choice, and, increasingly, in mainstream economics.

Dworkin (1981), Arneson (1989), Cohen (1989), and, to some extent, Sen (1985) are among a number of influential authors who have argued that inequality in the distribution of particular outcomes—such as incomes—is not the appropriate yardstick for assessing the fairness of a given allocation or social system. Despite important differences in nuance, these authors have all suggested that some outcome differences—which are attributable to differences in choices for which individuals can be held responsible—may be ethically acceptable. In this view, unacceptable inequalities reside in a logically prior space—of resources, capabilities, opportunities—for which individuals cannot be held responsible. 1 John Roemer (1998), for instance, calls those factors over which individuals have a measure of control, “efforts” (e.g. how long one studies, or how hard one works), while those for which they cannot reasonably be held to have any responsibility are referred to as “circumstances” (e.g. race, gender, or family background). Given this distinction, he defines “equality of opportunity” essentially as a situation in which important outcomes—which he calls “advantages”—are distributed independently of circumstances. 2 Such a distinction between inequality of opportunity and the more standard concept of inequality of outcomes is of interest to economists for at least three sets of reasons. First, there is an increasingly widespread normative view that it is inequality of opportunity, and not that of outcomes, which should inform the design of public policy. Inequality of opportunity is, in this view, the appropriate “currency of egalitarian justice” (Cohen, 1989). Public action need not necessarily aim to eliminate all outcome inequalities, but may be justified in seeking to reduce those that arise from unequal opportunities: “economic inequalities due to factors beyond the individual responsibility are inequitable, and should be compensated by society” (Peragine, 2004, p. 11). To the extent that this view, which is already popular among social choice theorists and political philosophers, gains traction among policymakers, will behoove economists to provide tractable empirical measures of the concept.

Second, if the degree of inequality of opportunity affects popular attitudes to outcome inequality, then it may affect beliefs about social fairness and attitudes to redistribution. These beliefs and attitudes may in turn affect the extent of redistribution actually implemented in society, and thus the level of investment and output generated: Alesina and Angeletos (2005) and Bénabou and Tirole (2006) provide examples of models where such beliefs and attitudes themselves play a key

1 Space constraints prevent us from exploring these differences in nuance here, but they have been reviewed extensively elsewhere (see, e.g. Roemer, 1993a). 2 Roemer phrases his definition somewhat differently. He argues that, if it were possible to partition the population into circumstance-homogeneous groups (which he calls “types”), and if the only variable that differed across individuals within each type was their effort level, then equality of opportunity would attain only if the distributions of advantage across all such groups were identical. Under Roemer’s assumptions, the requirement of identical distributions of advantage regardless of type is equivalent to stochastic independence between advantage and circumstances. Although this should be intuitively clear, we return to this argument more formally in Section 2.

Review of Income and Wealth © International Association for Research in Income and Wealth 2011 Review of Income and Wealth, Series 57, Number 4, December 2011 role in generating multiple equilibria, with very different objective economic characteristics.

Third, it has also been suggested that inequality of opportunity might be a more relevant concept (than income inequality) for understanding whether aggregate economic performance is worse in more unequal societies—and if so, why. In addition to the role of beliefs and attitudes to redistribution, it is possible that the kinds of inequality that are detrimental to growth (such as inequality in access to good schools, or to financial markets) are more closely associated with the concept of opportunities, while other components of outcome inequality—such as those arising from returns to different levels of effort—may actually have a positive effect on growth (World Bank, 2006; Bourguignon et al., 2007b). Perhaps one of the reasons why the cross-country empirical literature on inequality and growth is so inconclusive is that it conflates the two kinds of inequality. 3 In fact, a recent study by Marrero and Rodríguez (2009) finds that if one decomposes total income inequality into an “opportunity” component and an “effort” component, both terms have statistically significant coefficients in a growth regression estimated for 23 states of the United States in the last two decades. But while the coefficient on inequality of opportunity has a negative sign, the opposite is true for inequality of efforts.

But in order to make empirical use of the concept of inequality of opportunity—whether for the design of taxation and public expenditures or in the study of the determinants of cross-country growth differences—it is first necessary to measure it appropriately. The recent literature contains at least three different approaches to the measurement of inequality of opportunity. 4 Bourguignon, Ferreira, and Menéndez (2007a)—henceforth BFM—estimate a linear model of advantage (earnings) as a function of circumstances and efforts, and use it to simulate counterfactual distributions where the effect of circumstances is suppressed. By comparing the actual earnings distribution with different counterfactuals, they decompose overall earnings inequality in Brazil into a component due to five observed circumstance variables, and a residual. The circumstance (or inequality of opportunity) component is further decomposed into a direct effect and an (indirect) effect that operates through the influence of circumstances on the choice of efforts. Crucially, BFM seek to estimate the contribution of the five specific circumstances observed in their dataset: race, mother’s schooling, father’s schooling, region of birth, and father’s occupation. By imposing certain restrictions on coefficient signs and on their variance– covariance matrix, they estimate bounds on the possible biases arising from the omission of other, unobserved circumstance variables. The procedure is therefore interpreted as estimating the contribution of those specific observed circumstances to overall earnings inequality.

A second approach to decomposing overall inequality into an opportunity component and an “ethically acceptable” component is to rely on standard between-group inequality decompositions. Checchi and Peragine (2010)—

3 See Banerjee and Duflo (2003) on the inconclusiveness of that literature. See also van de Gaer et al., (2001) for an earlier treatment of inequality of opportunity in the context of intergenerational mobility.

4 Review of Income and Wealth © International Association for Research in Income and Wealth 2011 Review of Income and Wealth, Series 57, Number 4, December 2011 henceforth CP—show that if groups are defined by circumstance characteristics—so that they correspond to Roemer’s types—then the betweengroup component can be interpreted as an “ex-ante” measure of inequality of opportunity. Conversely, if groups are defined in terms of their relative position in the effort distributions across types, then inequality within groups (called “tranches” by CP) corresponds to an “ex-post” measure of inequality of opportunity. 5 The authors present both estimates for the distribution of earnings in Italy.

Finally, a third approach, associated with Lefranc et al. (2008), relies on stochastic dominance comparisons of distributions conditional on types for assessing whether inequality of opportunity is present in a society. These authors also propose a Gini of Opportunities index for the scalar measurement of inequality of opportunity.

This paper combines elements from the first two approaches, and shows that a variant of the parametric approach in BFM and the non-parametric ex-ante approach of CP are effectively alternative procedures for estimating the same quantity. For this to hold, however, it is necessary to interpret both estimates as yielding a lower-bound on the set of possible true measures of (ex-ante) inequality of opportunity. It is necessary, in other words, to treat the share of inequality associated with the circumstances one observes as a lower-bound on the share accounted for by all circumstances, observed and unobserved, rather than as the share corresponding to those specific observed circumstances. Under this interpretation, a variant of the index proposed by BFM and that due to CP are simply parametric and non-parametric alternatives for the measurement of (lower-bound) inequality of opportunity. 6 We derive this index from the pioneering definitions of equality of opportunity due to Roemer (1993b, 1998) and van de Gaer (1993), and define two versions for it: an absolute measure of the level of inequality of opportunity (IOL), and one measure that is relative to overall outcome inequality (IOR). Both versions are computed for six countries in Latin America—Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Panama, and Peru—using both the non-parametric and the parametric estimation procedures. Although the two methods tend to generate robustly similar results for large samples, the parametric approach yields more conservative estimates of the lower-bound for inequality of opportunity in smaller samples. The lower-bound estimates of the inequality of opportunity ratio (IOR) range from 25 percent of total inequality in household consumption in Colombia, to 51 percent in Guatemala.

Finally, we also define and compute opportunity profiles and opportunitydeprivation profiles for all six countries: these are rankings of types within society which may be of direct practical relevance for the implementation of the concepts of “equal opportunity policy” found in the literature, and to Roemer’s proposed

5 See the discussion in Section 2, as well as Fleurbaey and Peragine (2009), on the conceptual distinction between ex-ante and ex-post approaches to inequality of opportunity. 6 An added advantage of this approach is that it eliminates the need for the strong assumptions made by BFM to estimate confidence intervals around their coefficient estimates, so that those could be interpreted causally.

Review of Income and Wealth © International Association for Research in Income and Wealth 2011 Review of Income and Wealth, Series 57, Number 4, December 2011 criterion for assessing economic development. 7 The profiles are shown to vary substantially across countries (with ethnicity being fundamental in Brazil but much less important in Colombia, for instance).

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 relates our index of inequality of opportunity explicitly to both Roemer’s and van de Gaer’s conceptual definitions of equality of opportunity. It also defines the relative and absolute versions of the index, and describes some of their properties. Section 3 then discusses the two alternative procedures for estimating the index in practice: the non-parametric approach of CP, and (a version of) the BFM parametric approach. It also establishes that the index is a lower-bound estimator of the true measure of inequality of opportunity. Section 4 provides some information on the six household survey datasets used in our empirical application, and discusses issues of cross-country comparability. Section 5 presents the main empirical results, while Section 6 discusses the opportunity and opportunity-deprivation profiles. Section 7 concludes.

2. A Conceptual Framework Consider a finite population of discrete agents indexed by i ∈ {1,..., N}, where N is large. Each individual i is characterized by a set of attributes {y i, C i, e i }, where y denotes an advantage, C denotes a vector of circumstance characteristics, and e denotes an effort level. We follow Roemer (1998) in considering a single advantage variable (which we will later associate with household per capita income or consumption), and in representing effort as a scalar. 8 In this section, and for ease of exposition, we will also follow Roemer (1998) in treating effort as a continuous variable, while the vector C i consists of J elements corresponding to each circumstance j (for individual i), with the typical entry being C i j. Furthermore, each element C i j takes a finite number of values, x j, "i. 9 This permits us to partition the population into Roemerian types, i.e. population subgroups that are homogeneous in terms of circumstances. This partition is given by P ∈ {T 1, T 2,..., T K }, such that T 1 艛 T 2 艛... 艛 T K = {1,..., N}, T l 艚 T K = ∅, "l, k, and C i = C j, "i, j|i ∈ T k, j ∈ T k, "k. Naturally, the maximum

## J

possible number of types is given by K = ∏ x j. 10 It will prove useful to denote the j = 1 joint distribution of advantages and circumstances over the population by {y, C}, and the space of such distributions by W. The marginal distribution of advantages, of course, is given simply by the vector y = (y 1,..., y N ). Similarly, denote the space of possible population partitions P by L.

Review of Income and Wealth © International Association for Research in Income and Wealth 2011 Review of Income and Wealth, Series 57, Number 4, December 2011 In his original formal definition of equality of opportunity, Roemer (1998) defines the distribution of effort within each type T k, G ρ k (e) as “a probability measure on the set of effort levels, which are non-negative real numbers” (p. 10). Since he is primarily concerned with defining an equal-opportunity policy, or set of allocation rules, he adds a subscript to indicate that the distribution of efforts is conditional on some policy r. He denotes the advantage level enjoyed by a person in quantile π = G ρ k (e) of the effort distribution in type k, given policy r, as y k (p, r). His analysis is then couched in terms of seeking an equal-opportunity policy r*, which he ultimately proposes should maximize the average (over quantiles of the effort distribution) of minimum levels of advantage across all types, at each given quantile:

1 (1) ρ * = arg max ∫ min y k (π, ρ) d π.

ρ 0 k Although Roemer (1998) does not actually write down a formal definition of equality of opportunity itself—only that of the equal opportunity policy—his equation (1) has been widely interpreted to imply that equal opportunities would attain if the levels of advantage were the same across all types, at each and every quantile of the effort distribution: (2) y k (π, ρ) = y l (π, ρ), ∀ π ∈[0, 1]; ∀ T k, T l ∈ Π.

Equation (2) clearly accords with Roemer’s informal statement that “leveling the playing field means guaranteeing that those who apply equal degrees of effort end up with equal achievement, regardless of their circumstances. The centile of the effort distribution of one’s type provides a meaningful intertype comparison of the degree of effort expended in the sense that the level of effort does not” (Roemer, 1998, p. 12).

Now denote the cumulative distribution function of advantage in type k, under policy r, by F ρ k (y). Note that the effort rank (p) and the advantage rank must be the same within each type because, given circumstances, advantage is fully and monotonically determined by effort. Dropping the policy subscript r, which is not the focus of our analysis, and noting that y k (p) is simply the inverse function of p = F k (y), (2) then implies: (3) F k (y) = F l (y), ∀ l, k T k ∈ Π, T l ∈ Π.

This is presented as Roemer’s “strong criterion” definition of equal opportunities in Bourguignon et al. (2007b), and by Lefranc et al. (2008). 11 If equality of opportunity corresponds to a hypothetical situation in which advantage distributions are identical across types, then the measurement of inequality of opportunity must, in some sense, seek to capture the extent to which

11 Lefranc et al. (2008) refer to equation (3)—albeit obviously in slightly different notation—as “a compelling case of equality of opportunity [that] corresponds to the definition of equality of opportunity adopted by Roemer (1998)” (p. 517).

Review of Income and Wealth © International Association for Research in Income and Wealth 2011 Review of Income and Wealth, Series 57, Number 4, December 2011 F k (y) ⫽ F l (y), for k ⫽ l. An obvious first step would be to test for the existence of inequality of opportunity, by examining whether the conditional distributions of advantage differ across types. This is precisely what Lefranc et al. (2008) do, using stochastic dominance techniques and the associated statistical tests to compare conditional income distributions across types in a number of OECD countries, where the types are defined by the level of education (or, in a couple of cases, the occupation) of a person’s father.

Theirs is a very interesting approach to ascertaining whether or not individual countries, or other populations, could be described as having equality of opportunity. (In their sample, the null hypothesis of equal opportunities can be rejected for every country, except Sweden.) It also allows for a (partial) ranking of types within each country, relying on the dominance comparisons. This partial ranking is complemented by a scalar index for inequality of opportunity, which is based on a variant of the Gini coefficient, defined over mean advantage levels for each type and adjusted for “within-type inequality” (see Lefranc et al., 2008).

However, while this reliance on stochastic dominance comparisons across type-specific advantage distributions is desirable in terms of robustness, it does come at a practical cost, given usual sample sizes. Because the estimation of distribution functions (or generalized Lorenz curves) requires a reasonable number of observations within each type, the partition P of the population must perforce be quite coarse. Lefranc et al. (2008) work with K = 3 in all countries. This implies a rather limited treatment of inequality of opportunity, since any inequality within those three types is then associated with differences in efforts. These would include, for example, any income differences associated with gender, race, or birthplace that might exist within types defined solely on the basis of father’s education.

An alternative approach is to adopt a weaker criterion for the empirical identification of equality of opportunity, namely that mean advantage levels ∞ should be identical across types. If we define μ k (y) = ∫ ydF k (y), then this weaker criterion for equality of opportunity is written: (4) 0 μ k (y) = μ l (y), ∀ l, k T k ∈ Π, T l ∈ Π.

This criterion is consistent with Roemer’s original definition, given by equation (3), in the sense that it is always implied by that equation. Whenever (4) does not hold, so that the hypothesis of equality of opportunity is rejected empirically, we can be confident that the theoretical definition is not satisfied either (subject to the usual confidence margins associated with statistical inference): Since F k (y) = F l (y), "k, l ⇒ m k (y) = m l (y), "k, l, it follows that m k (y) ⫽ m l (y), $k, l ⇒ F k (y) ⫽ F l (y).

However, (4) is clearly weaker than (3), since two different conditional distributions may happen to have the same mean. It is possible therefore, that the empirical test in (4) will fail to reject the hypothesis of equality of opportunity even though it is false according to the original definition in (3). This kind of “type 2 error” in the empirical identification of equality of opportunity is not exclusive to this method, or to approaches that rely on the mean rather than the entire distribution. Precisely the same issue arises with empirical identification criteria based Review of Income and Wealth © International Association for Research in Income and Wealth 2011 Review of Income and Wealth, Series 57, Number 4, December 2011 on first-or second-order stochastic dominance. 12 The use of an empirical criterion for assessing whether or not equality of opportunity holds that is somewhat weaker than (3) seems to be the price to be paid for applying these concepts to The transition from equation (3) to equation (4) can therefore be justified on the basis of practical considerations: in practice, sample sizes are generally too small to allow for the estimation of type-specific distribution functions when the number of types becomes realistically large. There is also an alternative, and rather different, justification for moving from (3) to (4), which has to do with the conceptual distinction between the ex-post and ex-ante approaches to equality of opportunity. In the ex-post approach, inequality of opportunity is viewed as inequality among people who have exerted the same degree of effort, regardless of circumstances. Measuring this inequality would require aggregating outcome differences among people at the same effort quantile across types, for each quantile. Full equality of opportunity would imply equality at each quantile, and hence for the whole distribution (as in (3)).

The ex-ante approach, on the other hand, sees inequality of opportunity as inequality between groups of people who share the same circumstances (i.e. between types). Conceptually, the ex-ante approach does not require observing effort, or comparing individuals from different types at each percentile of their effort distributions. But it does require agreement on some valuation of the opportunity set faced by people in each type. Van de Gaer (1993) proposed that the opportunity set of each type could be valued by its mean level of advantage. 14 Full equality of opportunity, in this case, would imply equality at the mean (as in (4)).

In this paper, we are agnostic about whether one adopts the weaker criterion for equal opportunities (in equation (4)) on the basis of a conceptual preference for the ex-ante approach (and van de Gaer’s use of mean outcomes to value a type’s opportunity set), or for practical reasons to do with the difficulties associated with estimating full type-specific distributions for many types in most datasets. 15 Once one does accept (4) as identifying equality of opportunity, however, the measurement of inequality of opportunity must now seek to capture the extent to which m k (y) ⫽ m l (y), for k ⫽ l. A smoothed distribution, which we denote {μ ik}, was originally defined by Foster and Shneyerov (2000), drawing on the earlier inequality decomposition literature associated with Bourguignon (1979), Cowell (1980), and Shorrocks (1980). It was introduced to the measurement of inequality of opportunity by Checchi and Peragine (2010). The smoothed distribution {μ ik} is obtained from a distribution of advantages y and a partition P by replacing each individual advantage y ik with the group-specific mean, m k (y). So, with N individuals and K types, {μ ik} = (μ 11,... μ 1 n;...; μ iK,..., μ NK), 1 k k − 1 with μ gk =... = μ ik =... = μ hk ∀ k, g = 1 + ∑ n l, l = 1 and h = ∑ n l.

l = 1 The weak identification criterion for equality of opportunity in (4) and the definition of a smoothed distribution immediately give rise to a candidate scalar measure of inequality of opportunity, which maps from a joint distribution of advantage and circumstances {y, C} and from the associated partition P, to the non-negative real line. This index is given by q a: W ¥ L → ℜ +: (5) θ a = I ({μ ik}).

Associated with the absolute index q a, is a relative version of the index: q r: W ¥ L → [0,1]:
